title: Housing: build more, or something else?

turns.speaker: Devi
turns.text: Rents are up another nine per cent and the council's answer is a target of twelve thousand new homes.

turns.speaker: Ruth
turns.text: Targets aren't the problem. We've missed every target for fifteen years and nobody's been sacked for it.

turns.speaker: Marcus
turns.text: The supply argument is basically right though. Where cities built, rents rose more slowly. That's about as settled as this stuff gets.

turns.speaker: Devi
turns.text: More slowly, not down. Which is a hard sell to somebody paying two thirds of their wage.

turns.speaker: Marcus
turns.text: Agreed, and overpromising is how the argument loses. Building doesn't make housing cheap, it stops it getting worse faster.

turns.speaker: Ruth
turns.text: What frustrates me is treating it as one market. A luxury tower and a social flat aren't substitutes for the same person.

turns.speaker: Marcus
turns.text: There's filtering, though. Someone moves into the new tower and leaves a flat behind.

turns.speaker: Ruth
turns.text: Over about twenty years, on the studies I've seen. That's a generation.

turns.speaker: Devi
turns.text: Which is why social housing is the part that actually moves quickly, and it's the part we stopped building.

turns.speaker: Marcus
turns.text: I'd accept that. My objection is to people who say build nothing and fix it with rent control.

turns.speaker: Devi
turns.text: Rent control protects whoever's already inside and does nothing for anyone arriving.

turns.speaker: Ruth
turns.text: Which is most of the people in this conversation, so it polls extremely well.

turns.speaker: Marcus
turns.text: That's housing policy in one line, really.

points: Rents rose nine per cent and the council responded with a target of twelve thousand homes.
Ruth notes targets have been missed for fifteen years without consequence.
Marcus argues supply is broadly right: cities that built saw rents rise more slowly, though not fall.
Ruth objects that luxury and social housing are not substitutes; Marcus cites filtering, which Devi notes takes about twenty years.
Devi argues social housing moves fastest and is what stopped being built.
They agree rent control protects existing tenants while doing nothing for new arrivals, which is why it polls well.
